title: Why AI data centers are so controversial
description: AI data centers are being built faster than many towns can plan for, and the backlash has become a cross-party political fight. This explainer covers what a data center actually is, why one AI answer takes so much power and water, and who ends up paying for the power lines and the tax breaks. It shows why Texas Senate candidates in both parties now want the sales-tax breaks gone, and gives you four questions to ask if a project is proposed near you. Positions and figures are as reported in late October 2026, before the votes were counted.

scenes.say: Hottest week of the year. Everyone switches on their AC — the air conditioner — and the grey box on the pole hums. Then it gives out, and the street goes dark.
That box is shared, so one heavy user can mean the whole street splits the upgrade bill — or argues about it. Now picture that upgrade bill for a whole town's power supply.

scenes.say: I'm Thoma, your friendly neighbourhood tech imp. Let's poke at the grey box, and the buildings making it hum.

visual.sub: Why AI buildings start local fights

scenes.say: First, the plain version. A data center is a large building full of servers — powerful computers that answer requests — stacked on racks, plus storage, the gear that connects them, and cooling.
When you ask an AI something, your question travels to one of those servers. It does the work, sends an answer back — and heats up.
So the building needs two things, constantly: power to run the machines, and cooling to stop them cooking themselves. <laugh>
Large AI data centers can draw hundreds of megawatts. A megawatt is roughly what a thousand homes use on average — so hundreds of them is the power of 100,000 homes or more.

scenes.say: Why so hungry? Because an AI answer isn't fetched from a shelf. The machine builds it fresh, word by word, every single time.

visual.prompt: The best part of the trip was
visual.label: One word at a time, every time

scenes.say: Inside, one reply can mean billions of tiny sums — like pressing a calculator a billion times for a single paragraph. Each press is simple; there are just so many of them.
Multiply that by millions of people asking all day, and you need enormous buildings running flat out, day and night.

visual.text: Millions of asks, warehouses *running all night*

scenes.say: But here's where it gets weird. The computers are only half the story. The other half is where you put them.

visual.text: The hard part isn't the *computers*. It's where they go.

scenes.say: A company hunting for a site wants cheap land, a fat power line, water, fast internet, and permits that don't drag on for years.
It also wants a friendly deal. Towns often offer tax breaks — deals where the company skips sales tax on its equipment — hoping the jobs are worth it.

left.label: A discount for a new shop

right.label: A tax break for a company

scenes.say: The catch: the town simply collects less tax — and the real question is whether the project would have come anyway.
Meanwhile the neighbours notice the traffic, the noise from those cooling fans, the water — and sometimes a share of the bill for new power lines.
Why does a computer need water at all? Cooling. Some systems evaporate water to carry heat away, the way sweat cools you down.
It's often cheaper than the cooling your home AC uses, but it drinks the same river or groundwater the town relies on. That's the sore point.
Newer designs reuse the same water again and again instead. It's a real fix — just more expensive, and not everywhere yet.

visual.heading: The same water, again and again

scenes.say: So people show up at council meetings. And they don't all want the same thing.
Some ask for a pause. That pause has a name: a moratorium. It's not a ban — it's 'wait, let's check first', and how long it lasts is a choice.
Others want conditions: an independent check of the deal, a rule that the company pays for upgrades, or a local vote. A few want it gone.

And here's the surprise: this isn't one party's fight. In Texas, days before the 2026 election, both Senate candidates — the Senate is a national law-making body — want the state's sales-tax breaks gone.
Talarico is the Democrat — that's one of America's two big parties. He also wants water recycling and an 'AI dividend': a slice of tax on AI profits, handed back to the public.
Paxton is the Republican — the other big party. He wants data centers to pay for their electricity and for the extra power the state needs — and none of them in the countryside.
There's money behind this too. As of October 2026, Leading the Future — backed by tech investors and OpenAI's president — had spent $45 million in a year.

visual.label: Leading the Future's reported spend, one year

scenes.say: A group like that is a super PAC: a committee that can raise and spend huge sums to back candidates, without coordinating with them directly.

visual.text: Super PACs: big money, *no direct coordination*

scenes.say: But the biggest mistake is thinking this is only an environment fight. It's tax money, land, water, local control — and who gets to decide.
And no, not everyone who objects hates technology. Plenty of people want the project — with conditions.
If you want more of these plain-English breakdowns, subscribe — there's a new one every day.
So if one is proposed near you, ask four things: who pays for the power lines, how much water, what the tax break costs, and who signs off.
